plain_english: Even if all the greatest minds in history worked together on this problem, they could never fully express how amazed they are by human blindness. People won't let anyone set foot on their property. They'll grab stones and clubs over the tiniest boundary dispute. Yet they let others take over their lives. In fact, they actually invite people in to waste their time. You can't find anyone who wants to give away their money. But everyone gives away their life to countless people. We jealously guard our possessions from being wasted. But when it comes to wasting time — the one thing we should protect most carefully — we throw it around like it's worthless.
original_excerpt: Were all the brightest intellects of all time to employ themselves on this one subject, they never could sufficiently express their wonder at this blindness of men's minds: men will not allow any one to establish himself upon their estates, and upon the most trifling dispute about the measuring of boundaries, they betake themselves to stones and cudgels: yet they allow others to encroach upon their lives, nay, they themselves actually lead others in to take possession of them. You cannot find any one who wants to distribute his money; yet among how many people does every one distribute his life? men covetously guard their property from waste, but when it comes to waste of time, they are most prodigal of that of which it would become them to be sparing.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 3

plain_english: Let's imagine talking to an old man and saying: "We see you've reached the very end of human life. You're a hundred years old, maybe more. Now sit down and add up your whole life honestly. Tell us how much time you spent dealing with people you owed money to. How much on your lover. How much serving your king. How much managing your clients. How much fighting with your wife. How much disciplining your slaves. How much running around the city on errands. Add in the diseases you brought on yourself, and all the time you just wasted doing nothing useful. You'll realize you haven't actually lived as many years as you think you have."
original_excerpt: Let us take one of the elders, and say to him, "We perceive that you have arrived at the extreme limits of human life: you are in your hundredth year, or even older. Come now, reckon up your whole life in black and white: tell us how much of your time has been spent upon your creditors, how much on your mistress, how much on your king, how much on your clients, how much in quarrelling with your wife, how much in keeping your slaves in order, how much in running up and down the city on business. Add to this the diseases which we bring upon us with our own hands, and the time which has laid idle without any use having been made of it; you will see that you have not lived as many years as you count.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 3

plain_english: Look back and be honest with yourself. How often have you stuck to your plans? How many days went exactly as you wanted when you had complete control? How often did you stay calm and confident without losing your nerve? What have you actually accomplished in all this time? How many people have stolen pieces of your life without you even noticing? How much time have you lost? How much has been eaten up by pointless worry, empty pleasures, endless wanting, or small talk? How little of yourself do you have left? When you see this clearly, you'll realize you're dying too young — not because life is short, but because you've given most of it away.
original_excerpt: Look back in your memory and see how often you have been consistent in your projects, how many days passed as you intended them to do when you were at your own disposal, how often you did not change colour and your spirit did not quail, how much work you have done in so long a time, how many people have without your knowledge stolen parts of your life from you, how much you have lost, how large a part has been taken up by useless grief, foolish gladness, greedy desire, or polite conversation; how little of yourself is left to you: you will then perceive that you will die prematurely."
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 3

plain_english: What's the reason for this? People live as if they'll never die. You forget how fragile you are. You don't notice how much time has already slipped away. You spend it as if you had endless amounts, even though the day you're wasting on someone or something might be your last. You fear everything like the mortal you are, but you want everything as if you'll live forever.
original_excerpt: What, then, is the reason of this? It is that people live as though they would live for ever: you never remember your human frailty; you never notice how much of your time has already gone by: you spend it as though you had an abundant and overflowing store of it, though all the while that day which you devote to some man or to some thing is perhaps your last. You fear everything, like mortals as you are, and yet you desire everything as if you were immortals.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 3

plain_english: You'll hear many people say, "After I turn fifty, I'll finally have time for myself. When I'm sixty, I'll retire from public life." But what makes you think you'll live that long? Who says everything will work out exactly as you planned? Aren't you embarrassed to save only the scraps of your life for yourself? You're planning to enjoy your own mind only during the years when you can't do any real work anymore. How foolish to start living just when you have to die! What a stupid way to forget that we're mortal — putting off wise decisions until you're fifty or sixty, deciding that your real life will begin at an age most people never even reach.
original_excerpt: You will hear many men say, "After my fiftieth year I will give myself up to leisure: my sixtieth shall be my last year of public office": and what guarantee have you that your life will last any longer? who will let all this go on just as you have arranged it? are you not ashamed to reserve only the leavings of your life for yourself, and appoint for the enjoyment of your own right mind only that time which you cannot devote to any business? How late it is to begin life just when we have to be leaving it! What a foolish forgetfulness of our mortality, to put off wholesome counsels until our fiftieth or sixtieth year, and to choose that our lives shall begin at a point which few of us ever reach.
source_reference: On the Shortness of Life, Section 3
